focus: Exodus 1 shows Jacob’s household of seventy becoming a people that fills the land, just as God had promised, and then shows a new king of Egypt trying by every means to stop that growth. The chapter moves from blessing to forced labor, from forced labor to a secret order against Israel’s newborn sons, and finally to a public decree that every son be cast into the river.

sections.title: Jacob’s Family Becomes a People in Egypt
sections.summary: Exodus names the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, seventy persons in all, and records the death of Joseph and his generation. Yet the children of Israel “were fruitful and increased abundantly” until “the land was filled with them” (Exodus 1:7), the growth God had promised to Abraham.

sections.title: A New King Turns Israel’s Growth into Hard Bondage
sections.summary: A king “who did not know Joseph” (Exodus 1:8) fears Israel’s numbers and sets taskmasters over them to build Pithom and Raamses. The more Egypt afflicts them, the more they multiply, so the Egyptians make Israel’s lives bitter with hard bondage and make them serve “with rigor” (Exodus 1:14).

sections.title: The Midwives Fear God and Save the Sons
sections.summary: Pharaoh secretly orders the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill every newborn son, but “the midwives feared God” (Exodus 1:17) and let the boys live. God deals well with them, the people keep multiplying, and because the midwives feared God, He provides households for them.

sections.title: Pharaoh Commands Every Son to Be Cast into the River
sections.summary: When his secret order fails, Pharaoh commands all his people to throw every Hebrew son into the river. The chapter ends with this danger unresolved, and the next chapter begins with the birth of a son in the house of Levi.

1.brief: Exodus opens by naming the sons of Israel who came down to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household. The opening words tie the book directly to the end of Genesis, so the story of Israel in Egypt continues the story of God’s dealings with Jacob’s family.
1.explain:
“Now these are the names of the children of Israel who came to Egypt;”

Exodus opens with “Now,” a joining word in Hebrew that links this book to what came before. Genesis ended with Jacob’s family settled in Egypt and Joseph’s death (Genesis 50:22–26). Exodus picks up the same story. “These are the names” repeats almost word for word the list of Jacob’s family going down to Egypt in Genesis 46:8. The people about to suffer in Egypt are the family God chose and made promises to.

“The children of Israel” here means the sons of Jacob, whom God renamed Israel (Genesis 32:28). Within a few verses the same phrase will describe a whole nation.

“each man and his household came with Jacob:”

Each son came “and his household,” his wives, children, and servants. Jacob’s move to Egypt was a family move, made at God’s invitation: “do not fear to go down to Egypt, for I will make of you a great nation there” (Genesis 46:3).
1.notes: The Hebrew title of Exodus comes from its opening words, “These are the names.” The English title comes from the Greek translation and means “going out” or “departure.”

2.brief: The list begins with four sons of Leah: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah. Naming them one by one shows that the people about to suffer in Egypt are the real descendants of the patriarch to whom God made His promises.
2.explain:
“Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah;”

The list begins with four sons of Leah, in birth order: Reuben, the firstborn, then Simeon, Levi, and Judah. Each name stands at the head of a tribe that will play its part in Israel’s story. Levi’s line will produce Moses and Aaron (2:1; 6:16–20), and Judah’s line will produce David and, in time, the Messiah.

Naming the sons one by one shows that the people about to suffer in Egypt are the real descendants of the patriarch to whom God made His promises. Their names will appear again on the high priest’s shoulder stones and breastplate (28:9–12, 21).

3.brief: The list continues with Leah’s sons Issachar and Zebulun and with Rachel’s son Benjamin. Joseph, Rachel’s other son, is not named here because he was already in Egypt.
3.explain:
“Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin;”

The list continues with Issachar and Zebulun, Leah’s fifth and sixth sons, and Benjamin, Rachel’s younger son. Joseph, Rachel’s firstborn, is missing because he was already in Egypt (1:5). The list groups the sons by their mothers rather than strictly by birth order.
3.notes: The grouping by mothers follows the pattern of Genesis 35:23–26, where Jacob’s twelve sons are listed as sons of Leah, of Rachel, of Bilhah, and of Zilpah.

4.brief: Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher, the sons born through Rachel’s and Leah’s maidservants, complete the names. All twelve tribes are accounted for at the start of the book.
4.explain:
“Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.”

The last four names are the sons born through the maidservants: Dan and Naphtali through Rachel’s maid Bilhah, and Gad and Asher through Leah’s maid Zilpah (Genesis 30:3–13). Each one belongs fully to Israel. With Joseph already in Egypt, all twelve tribes are accounted for at the start of the book.

5.brief: Jacob’s descendants who came into Egypt numbered seventy persons, counting Joseph, who was already there. The small number sets up the striking growth the next verses describe.
5.explain:
“All those who were descendants of Jacob were seventy persons”

The family that came into Egypt numbered “seventy persons.” The count matches Genesis 46:27. Seventy was not a large number for a family that God had promised would become a great nation. That small beginning sets up the striking growth the next verses describe.

“(for Joseph was in Egypt already).”

The note in parentheses explains why Joseph was not in the list of names. He had been sold into Egypt years earlier, and God had used him to preserve the family during famine (Genesis 45:5–7).
5.notes:
The phrase “descendants of Jacob” reads literally those who came out of Jacob’s thigh, a Hebrew way of speaking about physical descent.

The Greek translation of the Old Testament reads seventy-five here and in Genesis 46:27. Stephen follows that count in Acts 7:14. The Hebrew text reads seventy. The two totals count the family differently, most likely by including or leaving out certain grandsons of Joseph.

6.brief: Joseph, his brothers, and that whole generation died. With the generation that knew Joseph gone, the family’s favored position in Egypt is no longer protected by living memory.
6.explain:
“And Joseph died, all his brothers, and all that generation.”

A whole era ends in one sentence. “Joseph died,” then “all his brothers,” then “all that generation.” The people who remembered how Joseph had saved Egypt were gone. With them went the living memory that protected Jacob’s family and gave them a favored place in the land. The stage is set for a change.

7.brief: Yet the children of Israel “were fruitful and increased abundantly, multiplied and grew exceedingly mighty,” until “the land was filled with them.” The piled-up words of increase echo God’s blessing on Abraham’s descendants and show His promise being fulfilled in Egypt.
7.explain:
“But the children of Israel were fruitful and increased abundantly, multiplied and grew exceedingly mighty;”

“But” brings a contrast. A generation died, but the family did not shrink. Moses piles up four expressions of growth: they “were fruitful,” they “increased abundantly,” they “multiplied,” and they “grew exceedingly mighty.” He then adds that the land was filled with them. The words echo God’s blessing at creation, “Be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28), and His promise to Abraham’s descendants (Genesis 17:6; 35:11). What God promised is happening, even in a foreign land.

“and the land was filled with them.”

The growth was so great that Israel spread through the land. The land here is Egypt, or at least the region of Goshen where Israel lived (Genesis 47:27). The family of seventy had become a people.
7.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “increased abundantly” is often used for swarming creatures that teem in great numbers (Genesis 1:20–21). It pictures abundant, almost uncountable growth.

8.brief: A new king rises over Egypt “who did not know Joseph.” The change of ruler leaves Israel without the standing Joseph once gave them, and the new regime will treat them very differently.
8.explain:
“Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.”

A turning point comes with “a new king over Egypt.” This king “did not know Joseph.” He may simply have never heard of him, or he may have refused to acknowledge what Joseph had done for Egypt. Either way, Joseph’s legacy no longer protected Israel. The family that had been honored guests became outsiders under a ruler who owed them nothing.

The text does not name this king. Exodus never gives the names of its pharaohs.
8.notes: Interpreters debate the identity of this king and the date of the exodus. An earlier date draws on 1 Kings 6:1, which places the exodus 480 years before Solomon began building the temple. A later date draws on the city name Raamses (1:11) and on historical arguments. Exodus itself leaves the kings unnamed.

9.brief: Pharaoh tells his people that the children of Israel have become “more and mightier than we.” The blessing God has given Israel now appears to Egypt’s king as a threat.
9.explain:
“And he said to his people, ‘Look, the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we;”

Pharaoh tells his own people what he sees: “the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we.” This is the first time Israel is called a “people.” The family has become a nation.

Pharaoh speaks with alarm. What God gave Israel as a blessing, Pharaoh sees as a threat. His words may exaggerate the danger, but they reveal his fear. The blessing God has given Israel now appears to Egypt’s king as a threat.

10.brief: Pharaoh proposes to “deal shrewdly” with Israel so they will not multiply, join Egypt’s enemies in war, and leave the land. He wants to keep them in Egypt and keep them small, which sets him against the very growth God has promised.
10.explain:
“come, let us deal shrewdly with them, lest they multiply,”

Pharaoh proposes a plan: “let us deal shrewdly with them.” He wants to act cleverly, using policy and pressure to control Israel. His goal is “lest they multiply,” to stop the very growth God has promised. Without knowing it, Pharaoh has set himself against God’s purpose.

“and it happen, in the event of war, that they also join our enemies and fight against us,”

Pharaoh names his fear. In a war, Israel might “join our enemies and fight against us.” A large foreign population inside Egypt’s borders could turn against the nation in a time of crisis.

“and so go up out of the land.”

He also fears that Israel might “go up out of the land.” He wants to keep them, not lose them. He wants their labor but not their strength. That is exactly the tension the rest of the story will resolve. God will bring Israel up out of the land.
10.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “deal shrewdly” is related to the word for wisdom. Pharaoh thinks his plan is wise, but his wisdom sets him against God.

11.brief: The Egyptians set taskmasters over Israel to afflict them with heavy burdens, and Israel builds the supply cities Pithom and Raamses for Pharaoh. The free family of Jacob is now forced into labor for Egypt’s king.
11.explain:
“Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with their burdens.”

Pharaoh’s plan begins with forced labor. The Egyptians “set taskmasters over them,” officials who supervised the work and drove the workers. The purpose was “to afflict them with their burdens.” The labor was meant to crush them, to wear them down so they would not grow.

The word “afflict” recalls God’s word to Abraham: his descendants would be strangers in a land not their own and would be afflicted, but God would judge that nation and bring them out with great possessions (Genesis 15:13–14). What God foretold is now coming to pass, and so will what He promised.

“And they built for Pharaoh supply cities, Pithom and Raamses.”

Israel was put to work building “supply cities” for Pharaoh, cities where grain and other goods were stored. Two are named: Pithom and Raamses. Both were in the eastern part of the Nile delta, near the land of Goshen. The free family of Jacob is now forced into labor for Egypt’s king.
11.notes:
The Hebrew word for “afflict” in this verse is the same root God used in Genesis 15:13: “they will afflict them four hundred years.”

The sites of Pithom and Raamses have been identified with various locations in the eastern delta. The name Raamses appears earlier, in Genesis 47:11, for the region where Joseph settled his family.

12.brief: “But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew,” and the Egyptians came to dread the children of Israel. Oppression cannot stop what God is doing, and Egypt’s fear only grows as its plan fails.
12.explain:
“But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew.”

Pharaoh’s plan fails. Oppression did not stop Israel’s growth. It seemed to speed it up. No king can undo what God has promised.

“And they were in dread of the children of Israel.”

As the plan failed, Egypt’s fear grew. The word “dread” describes loathing mixed with fear. The Egyptians felt sickened by the people they could not control. Egypt’s fear only grows as its plan fails.
12.notes: The Hebrew word translated “in dread” describes a feeling of disgust or abhorrence. It is used in Numbers 21:5 for Israel’s loathing of the manna.

13.brief: The Egyptians make the children of Israel serve “with rigor.” The forced labor becomes harsh and relentless.
13.explain:
“So the Egyptians made the children of Israel serve with rigor.”

The Egyptians respond by tightening their grip. They made Israel “serve with rigor.” “Rigor” means harshness, cruelty, ruthlessness. The forced labor became harsh and relentless.

The word “serve” is important in Exodus. Here Israel serves Pharaoh as slaves. Later God will demand, “Let My son go that he may serve Me” (4:23). The book moves from forced service to Pharaoh to the willing service of worship to God.
13.notes: The Hebrew word for “rigor” appears in Leviticus 25:43, 46, 53, where God forbids Israel to rule over a fellow Israelite “with rigor.” Israel was not to treat others as Egypt had treated them.

14.brief: The Egyptians make Israel’s lives bitter with hard bondage in mortar, in brick, and in every kind of field work. The repeated note that all their service was “with rigor” closes the description of slavery and shows how complete the oppression has become.
14.explain:
“And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage—”

The Egyptians “made their lives bitter.” The word “bitter” would be remembered every Passover, when Israel ate bitter herbs (12:8). The “hard bondage” was more than heavy work. It was slavery that crushed the spirit.

“in mortar, in brick, and in all manner of service in the field.”

Moses names the work: “in mortar, in brick,” the building work of making mud bricks and laying them, and “in all manner of service in the field,” agricultural labor of every kind. Every part of their lives was taken up by forced work.

“All their service in which they made them serve was with rigor.”

The verse ends by repeating that “all their service” was “with rigor.” The repetition closes the description of slavery and shows how complete the oppression had become. Nothing in their lives was free from it.
14.notes: The Hebrew words for “serve,” “service,” and “bondage” in 1:13–14 come from the same root. The repetition presses home that Israel’s whole life had been reduced to forced labor.

15.brief: The king of Egypt turns to a new strategy and speaks to the Hebrew midwives, named Shiphrah and Puah. Naming these two women gives them an honored place in the story while the king himself remains unnamed.
15.explain:
“Then the king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives,”

When forced labor failed, “the king of Egypt” turned to a new strategy. He spoke to “the Hebrew midwives,” the women who helped Hebrew mothers give birth. If he could not stop Israel’s growth by labor, he would try to stop it at birth.

“of whom the name of one was Shiphrah and the name of the other Puah;”

Moses records their names: Shiphrah and Puah. The king remains unnamed, but these two women are named. In God’s story, the faithful midwives are remembered while the powerful king is not.

There were likely more than two midwives for such a large population. These two may have been the chief midwives who represented the rest.
15.notes: “Hebrew midwives” can mean midwives who were Hebrews or midwives who served the Hebrews. Their names are Semitic, which suggests they were Hebrews themselves.

16.brief: Pharaoh orders the midwives to kill every Hebrew son at birth and let the daughters live. His policy has moved from forced labor to the secret killing of Israel’s newborn boys.
16.explain:
“and he said, ‘When you do the duties of a midwife for the Hebrew women, and see them on the birthstools,”

Pharaoh gives his instructions. When the midwives help “the Hebrew women” give birth and see them “on the birthstools,” they are to watch for the sex of the child. Birthstools were stones or a stool on which a woman sat or knelt to give birth.

“if it is a son, then you shall kill him; but if it is a daughter, then she shall live.”

The order is brutal: “if it is a son, then you shall kill him.” The killing was to happen at the moment of birth, at the midwives’ own hands. Daughters could live. Pharaoh may have thought that without men, Israel could not fight or grow as a nation. His policy has moved from forced labor to the secret killing of Israel’s newborn boys.
16.notes: The Hebrew word translated “birthstools” is literally “the two stones.” It most likely refers to the stones or stool used for support during childbirth.

17.brief: “But the midwives feared God” and did not do as the king commanded; they saved the male children alive. Their reverence for God outweighs their fear of Pharaoh, and their refusal protects the lives he ordered them to take.
17.explain:
“But the midwives feared God,”

To fear God means to revere Him, to take Him seriously as the One to whom they answer. Their fear of God outweighed their fear of Pharaoh. The king held their lives in his hand, but they knew God held more.

“and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the male children alive.”

Because they feared God, they “did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them.” They refused to kill. Instead they “saved the male children alive.” Their reverence for God outweighed their fear of Pharaoh, and their refusal protected the lives he ordered them to take. When a ruler commands evil, obedience to God comes first (Acts 5:29).

18.brief: The king calls for the midwives and demands to know why they have saved the boys alive. The question shows that his order is failing and that the women are now in danger themselves.
18.explain:
“So the king of Egypt called for the midwives and said to them,”

Pharaoh noticed that his order was not working. Hebrew boys were still being born and living. He “called for the midwives” to answer for it.

“Why have you done this thing, and saved the male children alive?”

He demanded, “Why have you done this thing?” The question shows that his order was failing and that the women were now in danger themselves. They had defied a king who had shown he was willing to kill.

19.brief: The midwives answer that the Hebrew women are lively and give birth before the midwives arrive. The text records their answer without commending it; what God honors is their fear of Him and their protection of life.
19.explain:
“And the midwives said to Pharaoh, ‘Because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women;”

The midwives give an answer: “the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women.”

“for they are lively and give birth before the midwives come to them.”

They explain that the Hebrew women “are lively,” vigorous and strong, and “give birth before the midwives come to them.” By the time the midwives arrived, the babies were already born, and the secret killing could not be done.

The text records their answer without commending it. Whether their words were partly true, entirely false, or a careful half-truth, Scripture does not say. What God honors in the next verses is their fear of Him and their protection of life. The passage does not give a general rule about deception.
19.notes: The Hebrew word translated “lively” means vigorous or full of life. It is related to the word for life used in 1:16 and 1:22 (“she shall live,” “save alive”).

20.brief: God deals well with the midwives, and the people keep multiplying and grow very mighty. God rewards their faithfulness, and Israel’s growth continues in spite of Pharaoh.
20.explain:
“Therefore God dealt well with the midwives,”

God rewarded them. He showed them favor and kindness. They had risked their lives to protect Israel’s children, and God did not forget it.

“and the people multiplied and grew very mighty.”

Israel kept growing all the while. Pharaoh’s second plan failed as completely as his first. God rewarded the midwives’ faithfulness, and Israel’s growth continued in spite of Pharaoh.

21.brief: Because the midwives feared God, He provided households for them. The women who protected Israel’s families are themselves given families, and the narrator repeats their fear of God as the reason.
21.explain:
“And so it was, because the midwives feared God, that He provided households for them.”

Moses repeats the reason: “because the midwives feared God.” Their fear of God is mentioned twice (1:17, 21), making it the center of their story.

God “provided households for them.” He gave them families of their own. The women who protected Israel’s families were themselves given families. God’s reward fit their faithfulness.
21.notes: The phrase “provided households” can mean that God gave them children and descendants, or that He established their families in some other lasting way. Either way, God blessed them with families.

22.brief: Pharaoh then commands all his people to cast every newborn son into the river and to let every daughter live. The secret order becomes a public decree against Israel’s sons, and the chapter ends with that danger hanging over the next generation.
22.explain:
“So Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying,”

Pharaoh’s third plan is the worst. He no longer works in secret. He commands “all his people.” Every Egyptian is now enlisted in the attack on Israel’s children.

“Every son who is born you shall cast into the river, and every daughter you shall save alive.”

The decree is public and total: “Every son who is born you shall cast into the river.” The river is the Nile, the source of Egypt’s life. Pharaoh makes it a place of death for Hebrew boys. “Every daughter you shall save alive” repeats the earlier order (1:16).

The chapter ends with this danger hanging over the next generation. The very next verses tell of a Hebrew baby born under this decree and of how God preserved him at the river.
22.notes: The Hebrew text reads simply “every son who is born.” The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Greek translation add to the Hebrews, which makes explicit what the context already implies.
